title: First aid for a burn
asks: how do I treat a burn
burned my hand on the stove what do I do
scalded with boiling water what now
should I put ice or butter on a burn
clothes stuck to the burn do I pull them off
bad burn from campfire no medic
wat to do for a burn
chemical or electrical burn first aid
when does a burn need a doctor
answer: Stop the burning first: get the person away from the source of the burn and put out any flames. A person on fire should not run: stop, drop and roll. Treatment given before the source is removed is ineffective and harmful.
If there are other life-threatening injuries, treat those first, then the burn.

Get medical help immediately for a deep burn: the skin looks white, blackened or charred, and there may be no feeling in the area. Rapid transfer to medical care is also needed for (WHO's list): serious burns to more than 15% of the body; burns of the hands, face, groin area or joints; burns that go all the way around a body part; a suspected inhalation injury (a burned airway, or smoke or hot gases breathed in); burns with other injuries; any burn in a very young or elderly person; and a burn in someone who already has a significant illness such as diabetes.

Suspect an inhalation injury (a burned airway) if there are burns to the face or neck, soot in or around the mouth or nose, singed facial or nasal hair, a dry cough, swelling of the lips or mouth, or a change in the voice, especially after a fire in a closed space. A burned airway can rapidly become blocked: watch the breathing closely and tell medical personnel as soon as possible.

Electrical burn: turn off the electricity, or if it cannot be turned off, drag the person clear with something that does not conduct electricity (rope, clothing, dry wood). High voltage or lightning may cause unconsciousness, difficulty breathing or an irregular heartbeat. Electrical burns typically affect the heart or the breathing: always care for heart and breathing problems before caring for the burns (Army survival manual). If the person is not breathing, start rescue breathing immediately; if there is no pulse, start CPR. The steps are on this library's card 'CPR for an adult'.
Chemical burn: carefully brush off dry chemicals with a clean, dry cloth, flush the burned area with large amounts of flowing water, and tell medical personnel immediately.

Cut the clothing around the burned area and gently lift it away. If clothing is stuck to the burn, cut around it and leave the stuck clothing in place. Remove jewelry and tight clothing from the burned area before the skin begins to swell.
Cool the burn with clean cold water, for 20 minutes if possible.
Deep burn (skin leathery and dry, looking black, white or brown): apply cool, wet compresses only briefly, and do not immerse the area in cold water.
Cover the burn with clean material such as a gauze bandage, a cravat or clean clothing.
Protect the person from hypothermia: keep them off the ground, on an insulated surface. Burn patients are particularly susceptible to hypothermia.
For pain, an over-the-counter pain reliever may be given when it can be done safely.

To judge how much of the body is burned (for the 15% in the list above), use the Rule of Nines for an adult: head 9%, each arm 9%, front of the torso 18%, back of the torso 18%, each leg 18%. The palm of the person's own hand is about 1% (the JTS burn guideline counts the hand with its fingers as 1%). Do not count skin that is only red, like a mild sunburn. A child's proportions are different: a larger head and smaller limbs.
Keep watching for life-threatening conditions and shock, check for other injuries, and seek medical aid. If possible, raise the burn above the heart to reduce swelling.
warnings: Do not use ice or ice water: it can cause more damage to the skin.
Do not put grease, butter or home remedies on a burn.
Do not remove charred clothing or material that is embedded in the burn.
Electrical burn: do not touch the person or the electrical source with your bare hands. You will be injured too.
Chemical burn: do not submerge the person in water. It adds to hypothermia and spreads the irritation.
If the person has a tourniquet on, do not cover it: keep it visible.

quotes.text: Burn care in TCCC is very basic. Eliminating the source of the burn should be the initial priority. Providing any treatment prior to removing the casualty from the source of the burn or extinguishing the cause of the burn will be ineffective and harmful to the casualty and casualty response personnel.

Catches on fire, the immediate action is to get away from the flame and smother the fire—do not run—Stop, Drop, and Roll. Suspect possible airway complications with burns to the face and/or neck; soot in the mouth and or nose; singed facial hair; or a dry cough.

A burned trauma casualty should be treated for all other life-threatening injuries first, following the MARCH-PAWS sequence, before addressing burns. Even if the skin is burned, trauma treatments can still be performed on or through it.

Full thickness burns are the most severe, these burns go through the entire thickness of the skin and can damage muscles or bones underneath. The skin may look white, blackened, or charred, and there might be no feeling in the area because of nerve damage. These burns require immediate medical attention and often need skin grafts to heal.

BURNS REQUIRING RAPID HANDOVER/TRANSFER: • Serious burns to >15% of body [See SKILLS] • Burns involving the hands, face, groin area, joints, or circumferential burns • Inhalation injury • Burns with other associated trauma • Any burn in very young or elderly people • Significant pre-burn illness (such as diabetes)

REMEMBER: Patients with serious burns to >15% of their body, burns involving the hand, face, groin area, joints, or burns that go completely around the body or a body part need to be transferred/ handed over for specialized care.
Inhalation injury Inflammation or oedema of the airways or lungs resulting from breathing hot gases or irritating chemicals (most commonly smoke inhalation in the setting of fire).

The body is divided into areas with each having a percentage of the total body surface area as follows: • Head – 9 percent. • Torso (front) – 18 percent. • Torso (back) – 18 percent. • Arms – 9 percent each. • Legs – 18 percent each. • Pubic area – 1 percent. • Buttocks – 1 percent.
General guidelines are that the size of the casualty's palm of the hand represents approximately 1 percent of the burned area.
For small wounds, calculate the size of the wound by using the patient's hand size (including fingers) to represent a 1% TBSA.
Note. First degree or superficial burns are not part of the burn percentage calculation and are rarely of medical significance.
Superficial burns affect only the outer layer of the skin, causing redness, pain, and mild swelling. They are like mild sunburn and usually heal within a few days without leaving scars.

Use the Rule of Nines body chart for adults and modified chart for children and infants (see figure). The body is divided into portions that each make up 9% of the total body surface. Children have different percentages due to the different body proportions, such as a larger head and smaller limbs (see figures).
The following may suggest inhalation or airway injury. –– Soot (ash) around nose or mouth, or singed (burned) nasal hairs –– Swelling to lips or mouth –– Voice changes
Burns involving the airway can rapidly cause airway obstruction.

Facial burns, especially those that occur in closed spaces, may be associated with an inhalation injury. These casualties should be monitored closely for potential airway issues. Do not place an NPA in a casualty with signs of inhalation burns. Notify medical personnel as soon as possible if an inhalation injury is suspected.

Electrical burn care consists of— • Eliminating the source of electrical burns. • Turning off any sources of electricity that have been exposed to the casualty (if applicable). • Using nonconductive material to drag the casualty away from the electrical source (if it cannot be turned off). Note. Types of nonconductive material include rope, clothing, and dry wood.

Do not touch the casualty or the electrical source with your bare hands. You will be injured too! High voltage electrical burns from an electrical source or lightning may cause temporary unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, or difficulties with the heart (irregular heartbeat).

In case of electrical burns, remove the victim from the contact with electricity. Electrical burns typically affect cardiac or respiratory systems. Always care for cardiac and respiratory problems before caring for burns.
If the casualty is not breathing, immediately start rescuing breathing and seek medical aid.
For patients without a pulse, follow relevant CPR protocols.
CPR is conducted using a specific technique to provide manual circulation support during cardiac arrest or when the heart has stopped beating effectively.

Thermal burn care consists of— • Stopping the source of the thermal burn and remove the casualty from the source of the burn. • Extinguishing any flames on the casualty, cut the clothing around the burned area, and gently lift away. CAUTION If clothing is stuck to the burn, ensure you cut around the clothing and leave the stuck clothing in place.

Chemical burn care consists of— • Eliminating the source of chemical burns. • Brushing off dry chemicals (carefully) with a clean, dry cloth. • Flush the burned area with copious amounts of flowing water to remove any liquid chemicals. • Applying a wet barrier (water-soaked gauze, clothing, or mud) with an occlusive dressing. • Advising medical personnel immediately.
Do not submerge a chemical burn casualty in water. This will greatly contribute to hypothermia and spread the irritation.
All burn care consists of— • Monitoring the casualty for life-threatening conditions. • Checking for additional injuries. • Treating for shock (if applicable). • Seeking medical aid.
Burn patients are particularly susceptible to hypothermia. Casualties should be kept off the ground and placed onto an insulated surface as soon as possible.
The addition of blood loss can cause the body's temperature to drop even when it is hot outside. The TQs should not be covered; keep them visible so medical personnel can easily see it.

Basic materials such as gauze bandage, clean clothing, and cravats can be used to cover burns and control bleeding. Cooling and cleaning burns should be done with available clean water, avoiding ice to prevent further skin damage.
Pain management, when possible, should include safe administration of over-the-counter pain relievers, and continuous monitoring for shock is essential.

Once the fire is out, assess the damage and begin to treat the burns. Initiate MARCH (see page 2-1) and protect the casualty from shock and hypothermia. Cool the burning skin with cold water for 20 minutes if possible.
Remove jewelry or tight clothing from the burned area before the skin begins to swell.
Do not use ice or ice water; this can cause more damage to the skin.
Do not put ointments, grease, petroleum jelly, butter, or home remedies on a burn.
Skin will be leathery and dry and can appear black, white, or brown in color. Do not remove any embedded charred clothing or material.
Apply cool, wet compresses to the burned area for a very brief to help reduce the body temperature. Do not use ice or immerse the affected area in cold water.
Be prepared to treat injured personnel for shock. If possible, elevate the burn above the heart to assist in reducing swelling and the likelihood or severity of shock.
Cool burned tissue immediately with cold water. If blisters are present, leave them intact, do not break them.

conflict: DRESSING, dry or moist (card only says 'cover with clean material'): JTS Burn Management PFC 2017 and JTS Prolonged Casualty Care 2021 say cover with clean, dry gauze or a clean sheet and always avoid wet dressings (hypothermia risk); ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says a clean, dry, non-adhering bandage for second-degree burns but cool, moist, sterile bandages for third-degree burns; ATP 4-02.11 (2026) says a wet barrier with an occlusive dressing for chemical burns; WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care 2018 says a non-adherent dressing that keeps the burn moist. OINTMENTS (card names only grease, butter, home remedies): ATP 3-50.21 says no ointments or petroleum jelly, yet in the same list allows antiseptic spray or aloe cream; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 says apply petroleum gauze to small superficial burns and a petroleum bandage to charred burns; JTS and WHO describe antimicrobial creams applied by medical providers. BLISTERS AND DEAD TISSUE: Ship's Medicine Chest main text and both JTS guidelines say leave blisters intact, and the Ship's Medicine Chest first-aid standard says 'not opening blisters or removing pieces of tissue'; but Ship's Medicine Chest main text also says remove loose and dead charred tissue with sterile tweezers, and WHO-ICRC BEC (trained providers) says carefully remove loose dead skin and broken, tense or infected blisters. COOLING: ATP 3-50.21 says cold water for 20 minutes if possible, but for third-degree burns only brief cool wet compresses and no immersion; ATP 4-02.11 gives no time. FEMA P-2064 (2020) has no burn first aid. BURN SIZE AND WHEN TO TRANSFER (lines added in revision): WHO-ICRC BEC 2018 lists 'Serious burns to >15% of body' among burns requiring rapid handover/transfer, and its fluid section starts fluids for full or partial thickness burns of 15% or more in adults and 10% or more in children; JTS Burn Management PFC 2017 says burns covering more than 20% of the body surface, or with smoke inhalation injury, are life threatening; ATP 4-02.11 gives no transfer threshold (its para 12-16 calls burns of greater than 20 percent 'extensive' when describing hypothermia prevention). The card shows WHO's 15%, the only figure given as a transfer rule and the lower one. HAND RULE (card shows both): ATP 4-02.11 para 12-5 says the palm of the hand represents approximately 1 percent; JTS Burn 2017 says the hand including the fingers represents 1%. The body-part percentages are ATP 4-02.11 para 12-4 (Rule of Nines), which also lists pubic area 1 percent and buttocks 1 percent (left out of the card); WHO BEC says the Rule of Nines chart is for adults and that children have different percentages. WHO's list does not define 'serious'; 'do not count skin that is only red' rests on ATP 4-02.11's note that first-degree burns are not part of the percentage. AIRWAY SIGNS (card lists all): ATP 3-50.21 gives face or neck burns, soot in the mouth or nose, singed facial hair and a dry cough; WHO BEC gives soot around the nose or mouth, singed nasal hairs, swelling of the lips or mouth and voice changes. ELECTRICAL BURNS, HEART AND BREATHING (sentences added to the electrical line after the re-review): ATP 3-50.21 (2018) Burns says 'In case of electrical burns, remove the victim from the contact with electricity. Electrical burns typically affect cardiac or respiratory systems. Always care for cardiac and respiratory problems before caring for burns.' ATP 4-02.11 (2026) para 12-10 names the effects (temporary unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, irregular heartbeat) but gives no action for them; JTS Prolonged Casualty Care 2021, written for medics, says 'For cardiac arrest due to arrhythmia after electrical injury, follow advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) protocol'; WHO BEC and the HHS manual have nothing on the heart after an electrical injury. No disagreement. What to do is not in the burn chapters, so the last two sentences rest on ATP 4-02.11 para 6-15 ('If the casualty is not breathing, immediately start rescuing breathing'), its CPR definition (para 6-45) and WHO BEC ('For patients without a pulse, follow relevant CPR protocols'). The reviewer's suggested wording was 'if the person is not breathing or has no pulse, start CPR'; the card instead follows the pulse rule of the card cpr-adult (not breathing: rescue breathing; no pulse: CPR), so that the two cards agree and nobody is told to compress the chest of a person who still has a pulse. Dependency for the owner: the line points to the card cpr-adult ('CPR for an adult'); approve this card only together with that one, or remove the pointer sentence. ORDER OF THE LINES: the Rule of Nines line was moved from before the airway line to after the cooling, covering, hypothermia and pain lines, on the reviewer's recommendation, so that estimating the size does not come before cooling; it now refers back to WHO's 15% in the transfer list. Its wording is otherwise unchanged.

review.notes: Re-review 2026-11-25 (claude-opus-5-5 xhigh). Pass. Previous finding fixed: the electrical line (now A5) says what to do for the heart and breathing: ATP 3-50.21 Burns ('Electrical burns typically affect cardiac or respiratory systems. Always care for cardiac and respiratory problems before caring for burns'), attributed, then 'not breathing: start rescue breathing immediately; no pulse: start CPR' (ATP 4-02.11 6-15, WHO BEC 'For patients without a pulse, follow relevant CPR protocols', ATP 4-02.11 CPR definition). That follows the cpr-adult pulse rule and never has a chest compressed while there is a pulse; the pointer uses the exact title 'CPR for an adult'. Recommended move done: the Rule of Nines line now follows cooling, covering, hypothermia and pain, and refers back to WHO's 15%; its wording is otherwise unchanged. All lines re-read against their quotes in context; transfer list, airway signs, chemical, thermal and electrical steps, warnings and the conflict record are still correct. Kind protocol; all asks answered; no PDF junk. Optional: A5 could end with cpr-adult's clause 'keep re-checking the pulse, and start CPR if it is lost' (high voltage and lightning can stop the breathing first and the heart later); not blocking here, because A5 states two separate conditions with no end point that excludes a lost pulse, and points to the CPR card. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 xhigh) Re-review 2026-11-25 (claude-opus-5-5 xhigh). Previous finding fixed: A3 now carries WHO BEC's whole rapid-transfer list, attributed, including serious burns over 15% and inhalation injury (also pre-burn illness); the new lines check out against their quotes in context: Rule of Nines (ATP 4-02.11 12-4), palm about 1% (12-5) with the JTS hand-with-fingers rule shown and attributed, only-red skin not counted (12-4 note and 12-3), child proportions and airway signs (WHO BEC), closed-space facial burns (12-17). The 15% vs 20% figures are in conflict. Remaining problem (point 4, safety-critical kit content left out): the electrical line A6 says high voltage or lightning may cause unconsciousness, trouble breathing or an irregular heartbeat, but never says what to do about it. ATP 3-50.21 (2018) Burns: 'Electrical burns typically affect cardiac or respiratory systems. Always care for cardiac and respiratory problems before caring for burns.' A2 says only 'other life-threatening injuries' first, which a lay reader may not apply to a stopped heart or breathing. Fix: add to A6 'Electrical burns typically affect the heart and breathing: always care for heart and breathing problems before the burns; if the person is not breathing or has no pulse, start CPR (see the CPR card)', with that quote. Recommended, not blocking: move A4 (Rule of Nines) below the cooling and covering steps so estimating the size does not sit before cooling in the step order. Kind protocol correct, all asks answered, no PDF junk. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 (xhigh), independent review 2026-11-24) Problem: the 'when to get help' list drops two items from its own quote. A3 is built on WHO BEC 'BURNS REQUIRING RAPID HANDOVER/TRANSFER', but it leaves out 'Serious burns to >15% of body' and 'Inhalation injury'. A large scald or flame burn is the main reason home care is not enough (shock, hypothermia), and A4 only says to watch a suspected burned airway and tell medical personnel. Fix: add 'large burns (WHO: more than 15% of the body)' and 'a suspected burned airway' to the rapid-transfer line (WHO BEC also repeats the list at 'REMEMBER: Patients with serious burns to >15%...'). Confirmed in context: ATP 4-02.11 ch. 12 (source first; trauma first; full-thickness signs; inhalation; electrical, thermal and chemical steps; do not submerge chemical burns; all-burn care; hypothermia; keep tourniquets visible; cover with clean material; no ice; OTC pain relief when safe); ATP 3-50.21 (stop, drop and roll; airway signs; 20 min cold water; jewelry; no ice; no grease or butter; charred clothing; brief compresses for deep burns; elevate); HHS (cold water, leave blisters). The dressing, ointment, blister and cooling disagreements are fully listed in conflict. No PDF junk in answer lines. Minor: A13 could name ibuprofen or acetaminophen only if a quote supports it (ATP says OTC only). Electrical burns: consider 'be ready to give CPR' since A5 warns of irregular heartbeat.
